summary: DLF builds and sells flats, low-rise homes, plots of land and small shop-offices, mainly around Delhi, and owns offices and shopping malls that it rents out. It also runs two hotels and some clubs.
description: DLF is a property developer. It buys land, gets building approvals, builds homes and offices, and sells the homes, plots and shop-offices to buyers who pay in instalments. Separately it keeps many of its offices and shopping malls and rents them out to companies and shops, which brings steady monthly rent. Homes are sold as flats in tall towers (condominiums), as low-rise independent floors, where each floor is a separate home, and as plots of land in planned colonies.
money: DLF earns money in two main ways. It sells homes, plots and shop-offices, and it collects rent from offices and malls (the report calls this its annuity business, meaning steady repeating income). It also earns fees for running common areas, and income from two hotels and clubs. Its costs are land, construction, approvals, selling and borrowing. A buyer’s payment is cash, not profit, and DLF counts the sale as revenue only when the buyer takes control of the home.
customers: Home buyers pay for flats, floors, plots and shop-offices, usually in instalments while the building is built. Companies pay rent to use office space, and shops and brands pay rent to sell in malls. Hotel guests and club members pay for rooms, meals and membership. The report highlights demand for luxury and super-luxury homes.
drivers: How many homes DLF sells and launches each year, how fully its offices and malls are rented, and what land, construction and borrowing cost.

groups.title: Homes: high-rise apartments and independent floors
groups.examples: A flat in a tall residential tower, or a floor of a low-rise building that is a separate home.
groups.explanation: These are DLF’s main homes for sale. The report calls the tower flats high-rise condominiums, and says independent floors are low-rise homes with one household to a floor.

groups.title: Plots
groups.examples: A piece of land in a planned residential colony.
groups.explanation: In plotted development DLF sells plots in a planned residential colony. General explanation: the buyer then builds their own house on the plot.

groups.title: Shop-cum-offices
groups.examples: A small unit that can be used as a shop or a small office.
groups.explanation: These are small commercial units, called shop-cum-offices, that DLF develops and sells, rather than renting out.

groups.title: Office buildings
groups.examples: Large office towers rented to companies.
groups.explanation: DLF develops offices and leases them to companies, which pay rent. The report says the rental portfolio is about 50 million sq ft, with occupancy of about 95% by area.

groups.title: Shopping malls
groups.examples: A mall where fashion, food and electronics shops pay rent.
groups.explanation: DLF develops retail malls and rents shop space to brands. Rent is the main income, as with offices.

groups.title: Hotels and clubs
groups.examples: A DLF hotel, and a club inside a DLF housing estate.
groups.explanation: DLF’s hospitality business, meaning hotels, clubs and food and drink, covers two hotels, The Lodhi and Hilton Garden Inn, and luxury clubs within residential developments.

basics.title: What is a sales booking, and is it revenue?
basics.text: General explanation: a sales booking is a buyer’s agreement to purchase a home. DLF counts revenue later, when the buyer takes control of the home. A booking is therefore not yet revenue, and the buyer’s instalments are cash received, not profit.

basics.title: What is the annuity business?
basics.text: DLF’s report uses annuity to mean income that repeats, mainly rent from offices and malls it owns and keeps. It also counts fees for running common areas and hotel and club income. It is steadier than selling homes because it does not depend on new launches.

basics.title: Why does it matter which company holds the building?
basics.text: Many offices and malls are held in a separate company, DLF Cyber City Developers Limited (DCCDL), in which DLF owns about two-thirds. Under accounting rules DLF does not add all of its sales line by line, but counts only its share of its profit.

steps.title: Keep land ready
steps.text: DLF builds on land it already holds, and the report says its land bank gives it growth without needing to buy more. Land cost, approvals and design are the first costs.

steps.title: Launch and sell
steps.text: DLF launches a project and takes bookings from buyers. Buyers pay in instalments as work progresses, and DLF calls what it receives collections.

steps.title: Build
steps.text: Builders and suppliers construct the towers, floors or plot infrastructure. Their bills and DLF’s borrowing costs are paid out while collections come in.

steps.title: Hand over
steps.text: DLF says it records revenue from a home at a point in time, when the buyer takes control of it. Revenue, profit and cash received are three different things and arrive at different dates.

steps.title: Rent and run buildings
steps.text: Offices and malls that DLF keeps are leased out. Tenants pay rent each month, and DLF also earns fees for running common areas.

specifics.title: Revenue arrives at handover, cash arrives earlier
specifics.text: DLF’s auditors flag that revenue from real estate projects is recognised at a point in time, when the customer gets control of the asset. A year with many bookings and instalments can therefore look different from a year with many handovers.

specifics.title: Offices and malls sit mostly outside the main numbers
specifics.text: The results presentation says DCCDL and other joint ventures are not consolidated line by line, and only DLF’s share of profit is accounted. DLF Limited’s consolidated revenue leaves out the rent earned inside DCCDL and other joint ventures, which the presentation reports separately.

specifics.title: Some projects are shared
specifics.text: The report describes The Westpark in Mumbai, DLF’s first launch in that city, as a joint venture in which DLF owns 51%.

specifics.title: Low-cost land held for years
specifics.text: The presentation says DLF’s land bank is low cost and that growth does not depend on buying new land.

watch: How many homes are booked each year, and how many are handed over?
Bookings come first, revenue later, so a gap between the two shows how much work is still to be recognised.
Compare sales bookings and collections in each results release with the revenue reported in the same period.
How full are the offices and malls, and how are rents changing?
Rent is the steady part of the business, and empty space earns nothing while costs continue.
Compare occupancy and rent for the rental portfolio year by year in the results presentation.
Which companies’ results are inside DLF’s own numbers?
Offices and malls sit mostly in DCCDL, which is not added line by line, so DLF’s own revenue can understate the group’s scale.
Read the notes on subsidiaries and joint ventures in the annual report and compare DLF’s consolidated results with DCCDL’s own results.
How much money is tied up in land and unfinished homes?
Land and building cost money long before buyers take their homes, and delays raise interest and construction bills.
Read the balance sheet notes on inventory and the project timeline sections, and compare with earlier years.
What could change demand for premium homes and offices?
The report highlights premium and luxury home demand and office leasing, so a downturn or new technology could shift either.
Compare launch pricing and sales bookings in each release, and read the outlook and risk sections each year.
risks: Rules on building and land use can change
The report says changes in development guidelines, environmental clearances, taxes and zoning can affect project viability and timelines.
The report says the evolving impact of artificial intelligence and geopolitical developments need monitoring, because they could change how much office space companies rent.
The report lists cyber security threats among operating risks that could interrupt business and weaken trust of customers.
The report’s cautionary statement lists competition, the ability to manage growth, the ability to attract skilled people and government policies as sources of uncertainty.
context: Zero gross debt in the development business
The report says DLF attained its stated objective of zero gross debt in its development business during 2025-26, ahead of the estimated timeline.
sources: DLF Limited Annual Report 2025-26 (copy filed with the exchanges)

stepsTitle: From land to a finished home and its rent.

quick.title: What it does
quick.text: DLF builds and sells flats, low-rise homes, plots and shop-offices, and owns offices and malls that it rents out. It also runs two hotels and some clubs.

quick.title: Who pays
quick.text: Home buyers pay for homes and plots, companies and shops pay rent, and guests and members pay for hotel stays and club use.

quick.title: How it earns
quick.text: It sells property for more than it costs to build, and it earns steady rent from offices and malls it keeps. Hotels, clubs and building upkeep add smaller amounts.

quick.title: What it spends on
quick.text: Land, builders and materials, building approvals, selling costs and interest on borrowing.

helps.title: Rent that repeats
helps.text: The report says its annuity business, mainly rent from offices and malls with occupancy of about 95%, is positioned to deliver steady growth, which does not depend on new home launches.

helps.title: Land already owned
helps.text: The presentation says DLF’s land bank is low cost and that growth does not depend on buying new land, which helps its margins on new projects.

helps.title: No gross debt in the development business
helps.text: The report says DLF reached zero gross debt in its development business, which leaves it more room to invest and to stay steady in weak years.

hurts.title: Inflation and interest rates
hurts.text: The report says inflation from energy shocks and interest-rate swings can influence customer sentiment, construction costs and capital allocation.

hurts.title: Conflict and uncertainty abroad
hurts.text: The report names the ongoing conflict in West Asia as a risk that can raise energy-driven inflation and affect buyers and costs.

hurts.title: Delays and supply problems
hurts.text: The report lists delays in finishing projects and supply chain disruptions as operating risks that can push back completion and raise costs.
